citations.title: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025.pdf
citations.quote: Self-reported burnout rose in every quarter of the review period. By October, 41% of emergency department staff met the review's threshold for high burnout, up from 29% in January.

citations.title: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025.pdf
citations.quote: Two wards piloted a compressed rota: four longer days, then three days off. After twelve weeks, burnout scores on both wards fell by roughly a fifth, sleep quality improved, and patient throughput stayed within normal variation.

citations.title: Moot court notes
citations.quote: Historical anchor: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default. It gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition and exempted continuous services.

citations.title: Moot court notes
citations.quote: Continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Working Time Code: rest periods, a cap on consecutive shifts, and averaging over a reference period. A shorter standard week sits inside that structure.

config.motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

messages.content: I see the downstream cost of chronic overwork every shift: burnout, poor sleep, people arriving at my department with problems that started as exhaustion.[1] A shorter week is a public-health intervention. Pilot programmes have reported lower burnout and better sleep without collapsing output.[2] We should take that signal seriously at national scale.

messages.content: Nobody here is pro-burnout. My problem is the word *nationwide*. The pilots I've seen were mostly voluntary, self-selected firms, often knowledge work,[1] where output is hard to measure and easy to reorganise.[2] A hospital, a bus network or a care home can't compress five days of coverage into four. They hire more staff or they cut service. Both cost money that somebody pays.

messages.content: Three points. One: "nationwide" need not mean "identical". The motion is about the default standard week, as we once did with the weekend.[1] Two: law already handles continuous-coverage sectors through shift rules.[2] Three: the burden of proof is on the status quo, a five-day week that was itself a policy choice, not a law of nature.
